newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BMW Paris briefing baffles analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BMW Paris briefing baffles analysts.

text.p: German luxury carmaker BMW AG baffled industry analysts on Tuesday by announcing an unexpected news conference at the Paris car show to discuss an "important strategic decision".

The carmaker had scheduled a background briefing over lunch for journalists attending the car show but then announced a Vformal news conference for 1100 GMT to be attended by BMW management board chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder.

Germany's Boersen Zeitung newspaper quoted a BMW official as saying the briefing was to discuss "an important strategic decision" but not about BMW's plans to seek state aid to help fund a 450 million pound ($702.2 million) British engine factory.
A BMW official in Paris told Reuters the briefing would not discuss BMW's plans to deal with new controversial German laws cutting sick-pay benefits that became effective on Tuesday.
The new law, which cuts sick-pay benefits to 80 percent of gross pay instead of 100 percent, sparked strikes on Tuesday at rival carmakers Mercedes-Benz and Adam Opel.

Industry analysts said they doubted the briefing was about the new engine plant planned by BMW and its Rover subsidary in Britain, which London's Sunday Times paper reported at the weekend was pressing London for aid.

"We are not likely to get a decision on the engine factory because they have only filed for the U.K. grant, so there is certainly not going to be a decision on that today," said one Frankfurt-based analyst who asked not be named.

The plant, which would create thousands of jobs in the Midlands region of Britain, would turn out 450,000 1.8 and 2.0 litre engines per year at full capacity. BMW is expected to decide in the next few weeks whether to build the plant.
But others said an engine plant deal could be announced.
"Some people are saying the engine plant will be built in the U.K. regardless of the U.K. aid decision," said Peter Schmidt at Automotive Industry Data in Britain.

BMW was not expected by analysts to announce any plans for a merger or acquisition since the carmaker was having such a difficult time incorporating Rover, which it acquired in 1994 from British Aerospace and Honda.
BMW has said Rover, which has been plagued by rumours that it was in worse financial shape than BMW admits, was operating according to plan and that Rover would show a profit in 2000.
Some analysts speculated BMW could announce a deal with Honda, seeking help to run Rover and also fulfil long-term rumours of a cooperation pact with the Japanese carmaker.
In addition, some analysts said BMW officials may announce a broad change in Rover's marketing plans that will see new Rover cars advertised as a uniquely British product.
Advertising industry publications have reported that Rover would change its marketing plan before the launch of its next range of cars, due to be unveiled through 1997 and 1998.
The cars are expected to be radicaly different in appearance and will distance Rover from BMW.
Some analysts also said new Rover chief executive Walter Hasselkus may announce more management changes following his appointment at the carmaker in early September.
"It may be more fundamental changes in responsibility over Rover. It could well be that they have decided to put in another liason between BMW and Rover," said one analyst.

"What they basically need is a hachet man in the sense that BMW has been so successful in the past that they really have forgotten how to take tough decisions because they did not have to make them," he said. ($1=.6408 Pound)
